question.text: Why is the act of an issuer giving out misinformation that affects market price considered fraud even if investors did not directly rely on the statement?

answer.text: Because the issuer has a fiduciary duty regardless of whether anyone trades
Because investors are effectively misled through the market price impact, even though they did not rely on the statement itself or anything derived from it other than the market price
Because SEBI regulations do not require investor reliance for any type of fraud
Because the company's market capitalization is affected

explanation.text: The Logic: Regulation 2(1)(c)(i) of the PFUTP Regulations, as set out in workbook pages 48 and 144, treats issuer misinformation that affects market price as fraud because investors are effectively misled even though they did not rely on the statement itself or anything derived from it other than the market price. The Trap: Option C overstates the position by saying SEBI regulations never require investor reliance; the source ties the no-direct-reliance reasoning specifically to this market-price clause. Option A (fiduciary duty) and Option D (market capitalization) are not the rationale used in the regulation. Note: The key element from the source is the market-price transmission of misinformation, not any broader doctrinal label.
